Professor of Forest Management Email | ResearchGate
Welcome! I am an Assistant Professor at the École de foresterie, Université de Moncton (Edmundston). My research focuses on understanding how climate change is reshaping forests, with an emphasis on landscape-level forest management, spatial analytics, and data-driven modeling. I develop and apply tools to quantify climate impacts and support adaptive management strategies for resilient forest ecosystems across North America.

title: Our Team
text:
PhD Students



Joanie Dubé
Supervision 2026 - Ongoing
PhD Student Bio: Joanie is a doctoral researcher at the École de foresterie, where she is pursuing a PhD in Life Sciences at Université de Moncton. As part of the TransX project, she studies the performance of tree populations originating from different regions of North America and transplanted along a climatic gradient as part of an assisted migration approach. Her research focuses on growth, survival, and functional traits to better understand the capacity of tree populations to adapt to new climatic conditions. This knowledge will contribute to the development of silvicultural strategies adapted to climate change. Originally from Edmundston, New Brunswick, Joanie holds a Bachelor of Science in Biology from Université de Moncton and a Master’s degree in Environmental Sciences from the Université du Québec à Montréal. She has more than 10 years of experience in ecology and environmental project management, particularly in wildlife conservation, ecosystem management, and land-use planning. She also teaches wildlife ecology at Université de Moncton.





Nicolas Girard
Co-Supervision 2026 - Ongoing
PhD Student Bio: Originally from the Lac-Saint-Jean region of Quebec, Nicolas obtained his BSc in Forest Management and MSc in Forest Sciences from the Université de Moncton. His research focuses on ecological forestry under climate change, with a particular interest in using forest modelling and decision-support systems to translate natural disturbance regimes into practical management strategies at the landscape level. Before beginning his PhD at UNB, he worked as a professional forester managing the Université de Moncton’s Experimental Forest and teaching forestry field courses. In his spare time, Nicolas enjoys fishing, gaming, and listening to 80s rock music.

title: Join the Lab
text:
If you are interested in forest management, climate change adaptation, or spatial analytics, we would love to hear from you.


Assistant Professor Email: cedric.albert@umoncton.ca





We are always looking for motivated students to join the École de foresterie at the Edmundston campus. The Université de Moncton is a French-language university; therefore, candidates are expected to have functional proficiency in French for presentations, reports, exams, and interactions with other students. However, research activities and publications may be conducted in English, according to the candidate’s preference.


Our undergraduate program provides a strong foundation in forest ecology, geomatics, and sustainable management.
Learn More



We offer thesis-based Master’s projects focusing on climate change impacts and adaptive silviculture. Students benefit from close proximity to the Acadian forest and strong ties with industrial partners.
Learn More



We offer thesis-based doctoral projects focused on forestry research, including climate change impacts, forest management, and adaptive silviculture. The Ph.D. program also provides opportunities to supervise and collaborate with students working on applied forestry projects.
Learn More





Research is often a multi-institutional effort. We co-supervise PhD students registered at our partner institutions. You can still reach out to Dr. Albert to arrange a project and a supervision team.






PhD in Forestry



Prospective PhD or MScF students can also pursue doctoral or master research under the co-supervision of Dr. Albert while registered any other Universities. We already have collaborators at:

Université Laval (FFGG)
University of New Brunswick (ForEM)

title: Climate Change and Forest Ecosystems Lab
text:
École de foresterie · Université de Moncton, Edmundston



We study how a changing climate is reshaping the forests of New Brunswick and eastern North America, and we build the models and planning tools that forest managers need to adapt.

Our research Join the lab

title: Climate Change and Forest Ecosystems Lab
text:
What we work on


Climate impacts on stands
Process-based growth models and tree-ring data tell us how heat and drought stress are changing growth, survival and species composition in the Acadian forest.


Landscape-level planning
We bring climate projections into long-term strategic forest planning, so that wood supply forecasts and harvest schedules reflect the forest we will actually have.


Adaptive silviculture
Field experiments on thinning, seed sources and assisted migration test which practices keep stands productive and resilient under warmer, drier conditions.


Four projects are currently active: TransX, ThiRST, ALERT and CLIMCON, each open to graduate students.
See all projects

title: Climate Change and Forest Ecosystems Lab
text:
Where we are
The lab is part of the École de foresterie at the Université de Moncton’s Edmundston campus, in northwestern New Brunswick. We work closely with industry, government and university partners across the Maritimes and Quebec.

title: Research
text:
Our projects combine long-term field trials with modelling and remote sensing. Most are run with industry and university partners, and every project below has room for a graduate student.






Looking for a thesis project? All four projects are open to MSc and PhD candidates. See Join the lab for how to get in touch.




TransXThiRSTALERTCLIMCON



Transborder experimental assessment of warming vulnerability in northeastern tree species and their assisted migration potential

Data · Collection ongoing Funding · Funded Student · Position open



TransX tests how northern tree species and their seed sources respond to warming. Trees from across their natural ranges are planted along a broad temperature gradient in eastern Canada and the US. The goal is to identify the genetic stock that will keep plantations productive and the regional wood supply secure as the climate warms.

Partners and links

Project lead website (D’Orangeville Lab)
Silva21 research portal







Distribution of TransX experimental sites.






Objectives

Assess the warming tolerance of key hardwood and softwood species and populations to inform adaptive silviculture.
Assess the cold tolerance of southern populations to guide assisted migration and revisions to seed transfer zones.
Quantify genetic control of growth and survival across the temperature range for well-known improved progenies.





Large-scale experimental assessment of pre-commercial thinning to reduce drought vulnerability

Data · Collection ongoing Funding · Not currently funded Student · Position open



Drought events are projected to become more frequent and more severe, with direct consequences for the growth of commercial softwoods. ThiRST, established in 2022, asks whether pre-commercial thinning can reduce drought stress in white spruce: with fewer stems competing, each tree may have more water available.
The trial is located in the Black Brook district of New Brunswick, on land managed by J.D. Irving Ltd.





Field view of the ThiRST experiment.






Objectives

Assess the vulnerability of white spruce plantations to water deficit.
Evaluate how well pre-commercial thinning reduces white spruce stress under water deficit.





Acadian Land-use Evaluation of Resource Trade-offs

Data · Available Funding · Partly funded Student · Position open



Land on the Acadian Peninsula is under growing pressure from forestry, blueberry production and peat extraction. ALERT tracks how land use has changed across the peninsula and what those changes mean for forest ecosystems, agriculture and regional planning.





Part of the Acadian Peninsula seen by Sentinel-2, 2025.






Objectives

Quantify long-term land-use and land-cover change across the Acadian Peninsula (forest, blueberry fields, peatlands) using multi-temporal satellite imagery and spatial analysis.
Identify the main biophysical and socio-economic drivers of that change and assess what it means for forest ecosystems and sustainable land use in the region.





CLIMate impacts on CONifer plantations

Data · Available Funding · Not currently funded Student · Position open



How do thinning and climate together shape the productivity of white spruce plantations? CLIMCON combines growth modelling, dendroclimatology and climate projections to follow stand structure, thinning intensity and climate across past, present and future conditions.





Black spruce plantation.






Objectives

Project the future growth and timber yield of white spruce plantations under climate change scenarios, and evaluate how climate change may alter silvicultural outcomes in New Brunswick and Quebec.

title: Research Projects
text:
Navigate through our active research initiatives using the tabs below.

TransXThiRSTALERTCLIMCON



Transborder experimental assessment of warming vulnerability in northeastern tree species and their assisted migration potential




Project Overview
The TransX project addresses the risks posed by climate change to our northern forests. By evaluating tree species and provenances across a large warming gradient, we aim to identify the genetic stock that will maintain and improve productivity and ensure the resilience of the overall wood supply in Eastern Canada and the US.

Data Status: Collection Ongoing


Student Status: Looking for Candidate


Funding Status: Funded



Partners & Links

Project Lead Website
Silva21 Research Portal







Figure: Distribution of TransX experimental sites.






Main Project Objectives

Objective 1: Assess the warming tolerance of key natural hardwood and softwood species and populations to inform adaptive silviculture strategies.
Objective 2: Assess the cold tolerance of southern populations to inform assisted migration and changes in seed transfer zones.
Objective 3: Quantify genetic control of growth and survival across temperature range for well-known improved progenies.






Large-scale experimental assessment of pre-commercial thinning to reduce the vulnerability of drought




Project Overview
The ThiRST experiment, established in 2022, is a silvicultural study designed to evaluate whether pre-commercial thinning can help mitigate drought-related stress in white spruce stands. This question is increasingly relevant for the forestry sector, as projections indicate a rise in both the frequency and intensity of drought events, with potential impacts on the growth and yield of commercially important softwood species. By reducing stand density, pre-commercial thinning may improve water availability to individual trees and enhance their resilience. The trial is located in the Black Brook district of New Brunswick on land managed by J.D. Irving Ltd.

Data Status: Collection Ongoing


Student Status: Looking for Candidate


Funding Status: Not Currently Funded







Figure: Field view of the ThiRST experiment.






Main Project Objectives

Objective 1: To assess the vulnerability of white spruce plantations to water deficit.
Objective 2: To evaluate the effectiveness of pre-commercial thinning in reducing white spruce stress under water deficit.






Acadian Land-use Evaluation of Resource Trade-offs




Project Overview
This project examines how land use is evolving across the Acadian Peninsula and the implications of these changes for forest ecosystems, agricultural production, and other competing land uses such as peatland development. As pressures on land intensify in eastern Canada, understanding the balance between forest management, blueberry cultivation, peat extraction, and other uses has become critical for sustainable regional planning.

Data Status: Data available


Student Status: Looking for Candidate


Funding Status: Partly Funded







Figure: Partial view of the Acadian Peninsula from Sentinel-2 in 2025.






Main Project Objectives

Objective 1: Quantify and characterize long-term land-use and land-cover changes across the Acadian Peninsula (e.g., forest, agriculture/blueberries, peatlands) using multi-temporal remote sensing data and spatial analysis.
Objective 2: Identify and assess the main biophysical and socio-economic drivers of land-use change and evaluate their implications for forest ecosystems and regional land-use sustainability.






CLIMate impacts on CONifer plantations




Project Overview
This research examines how silvicultural practices and climate variability jointly influence the productivity of white spruce plantations in eastern Canada. It integrates growth modeling, dendroclimatology, and climate change projections to understand how stand structure, thinning intensity, and climatic conditions interact across past, present, and future time horizons.

Data Status: Data available


Student Status: Looking for Candidate


Funding Status: Not Currently Funded







Figure: Black spruce plantation.






Main Project Objectives

Objective 1: Project future growth and timber yield of white spruce plantations under climate change scenarios, and evaluate how climate change may alter silvicultural outcomes and productivity in New Brunswick and Quebec.
